title: Attar's birds
hookLine: The Conference of the Birds, where thirty birds seek their king and find themselves

cards: All the birds of the world gather for a meeting. They have no king, and they've decided they need one. A small bird with a crest on its head steps forward: the hoopoe.
A king exists, it tells them, far away behind a great mountain, and its name is the Simorgh. The road is long and dangerous. Who will come?
Then, one by one, the excuses. The nightingale can't leave the rose it loves. The duck can't leave the water.
The hawk is happy serving a human king. Each reason sounds perfectly sensible. This is the opening of a long Persian poem by Attar.

teach.h: A HOOPOE GUIDES, AS IN THE QUR'AN.
teach.b: The poem is called Mantiq al-Tayr, often translated the Conference of the Birds, or the Speech of the Birds. The title echoes the Qur'an, where Solomon says he has been taught the speech of birds.
And the hoopoe is no random choice: in the Qur'an's story, a hoopoe brings Solomon news of the Queen of Sheba. So Attar's guide already carried messages in scripture.
The hoopoe answers every excuse with a story, and slowly the birds set out.
The way, the poem says, crosses seven valleys: the search, love, knowledge, detachment, unity, bewilderment, and finally poverty and annihilation.
Many birds turn back. Many die on the road. Only thirty arrive.
In Persian, thirty birds is si morgh. The king they searched for is the Simorgh.

teach.h: THEY SEE THE KING, AND THEMSELVES.
teach.b: When the curtain lifts, they look at the Simorgh and see themselves; they look at themselves and see the Simorgh.
Readers in the Sufi tradition hear in this the soul's journey to God, where the seeker who has let go of self finds the One sought was nearer than imagined. What that means has been argued over.
In the poem, the Simorgh speaks of itself as a mirror, and many Sufi readers stress that the birds do not become God: what shines in a mirror is not the mirror.
Some link it to the verse in Pickthall's translation: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." A long road, to find what was close all along.

how: Attar's Conference of the Birds is read and taught in Sufi circles and Persian literature classes as an allegory of the seeker's journey to God, and it is often staged as theater and retold for children.

games.q: you're one of the birds. the hoopoe says the road crosses seven valleys and many won't survive it. your nest is warm. what do you do?
o: stay home: the nest is good enough.
send another bird to report back.
games.why: the poem's birds who arrive are the ones who kept going. only thirty reach the end, and they find themselves in the Simorgh.

practice: Bring to mind something you're searching for right now: peace, purpose, God, or simply a better way to live this year.

Then ask the hoopoe's question, what is my excuse, the rose I can't leave or the water I'm comfortable in, and name it honestly, without scolding yourself. If you pray, hold your search before God in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Attar's birds. The birds of the Conference, led by the hoopoe through seven valleys, until thirty of them reach the Simorgh and find themselves in its mirror. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: the Simorgh, the great bird-king; si morgh means thirty birds.
